extracted.intended_audience: high-school mathematics competitors, coaches, and problem-solvers (China Mathematical Competition participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of contest problems and worked solutions from the China Mathematical Competition (2004). Includes the contest structure, scoring allocation, and problem-specific conventions used for counting and reasoning in solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam structure and scoring (Parts I–III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part I Multiple-choice Questions (Questions 1 to 6 carry 6 marks each). Part II Short-answer Questions (Questions 7 to 12 carry 6 marks each). Part III Word Problems (Questions 13 to 15 carry 20 marks each).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines the contest format and marks-per-question allocation used to assess contestants; use when planning time/effort in the exam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence rule for circular arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: If one arrangement of the balls is congruent to another after a rotation or a reflection, the two arrangements are regarded as the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When counting distinct circular arrangements, identify and collapse arrangements equivalent under rotation and reflection (i.e., count inequivalent up to dihedral symmetries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'lucky number' (problem-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural number a is called a 'lucky number' if the sum of its digits is 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition as the selection criterion for constructing the ordered sequence of 'lucky numbers' and for counting how many of each digit-length meet the property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting positive integer solutions (standard combinatorial formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of nonnegative (or positive) integer solutions of x1 + x2 + ... + xk = m is given by standard binomial-coefficient formulas (used repeatedly in solutions). Example usage: number of nonnegative integer solutions = C(m + k - 1, k - 1); number of positive integer solutions = C(m - 1, k - 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this standard combinatorial identity whenever partitioning total integer resources (time, digits sum, etc.) among variables in contest problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting circular permutations of n distinct elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A circular arrangement of n distinct elements has (n-1)! linear orderings up to rotation; when reflections are also identified, divide further by 2 (if applicable). (Example in text: 9 distinct balls on a circle → 8! arrangements before factoring reflections.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the (n-1)! baseline and then account for reflection symmetry if the problem statement regards reflected arrangements as identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convention for treating congruent arrangements in probability problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing probability over arrangements, treat arrangements equivalent under rotation/reflection as the same sample point (reduces denominator appropriately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust both numerator (favourable arrangements) and denominator (total distinct arrangements) according to the chosen equivalence to compute probabilities correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-selection / syllabus-level guidance (remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: 'Problems concerning probability theory first appeared in the National High School Mathematics Competition. Problems are not too difficult. Topics such as derivative and its applications have already appeared in high school textbooks. These topics will also appear in mathematics competitions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates expected topic scope and difficulty level for these contest problems—suitable for advanced high-school syllabus topics (basic calculus, elementary probability, combinatorics, geometry, number theory). Useful for constructing practice curricula and selecting problems appropriate to the competition level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence / uniqueness condition for minimal-arrangement objective (problem-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the 9-ball circle problem: the minimum value of S (sum of absolute differences of neighboring ball numbers) occurs exactly when, along each of the two arcs from 1 to 9, the numbers strictly increase from 1 to 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When optimizing sums defined along cyclic orderings, characterize equality/minimizer conditions explicitly (here: monotone increasing order on each arc) to count extremal arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution/time divisibility constraints (problem-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the training-matches problem: at any moment during a match one and only one player is on the field; total time (in minutes) on the field for each of A1, A2, A3, A4 is divisible by 7; total time for each of A5, A6, A7 is divisible by 13.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the problem as finding positive integer solutions of x1+...+x7=270 under divisibility constraints; reduce by factoring out the divisors (set xi=7 yi or 13 yj) and count compositions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard algebraic/number-theoretic facts as constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Several solutions rely on standard number-theory facts (e.g., order of an integer modulo m, congruence manipulations) and algebraic identities; these are treated as permissible steps in contest solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contest solutions may invoke classical lemmas (order modulo m, modular congruences, factorization, Vieta relations) without expansive justification, but must state necessary consequences (e.g., existence of minimal order u with 3^u ≡ 1 (mod 104)).
